task.goal: Create a low-pressure way for a repair café to celebrate failed repair attempts as useful learning rather than shame.
hard_constraints: Four volunteers have a table, paper and a small display board for one monthly event.
No photos or names without explicit consent, no prizes or leaderboards, and no unsafe repair advice.
Participation is optional, usable without public speaking, and does not slow the queue substantially; pilot with observation and opt-out checks.
task.available_resources: Existing repair notes with permission to summarize anonymously.
task.expected_result: A concrete ritual and evaluation of learning versus embarrassment.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Useful Ending
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make an unsuccessful repair produce a small, optional learning record. The mechanism is to give the attempt a useful endpoint: an observation or boundary worth remembering, even when the item remains broken.

At handback, a volunteer offers a paper slip: “Still broken; now we know…” The owner can tick “one possibility ruled out,” “a limit identified,” “a question clarified,” or “nothing clear yet,” then optionally add a sentence. No explanation aloud is required. Blank slips are fine. The owner keeps the slip unless they separately consent to an anonymous summary appearing on the board. A volunteer reviews any shared wording, removing identifying details and procedural repair advice. The board heading reads “Useful endings this month.” Permitted existing notes can supply a few examples without implying that their owners joined this ritual.

Four volunteers use one table corner for slips and the small board for summaries. The handback volunteer makes the offer; another reviews contributions during quiet moments. Folding paper creates separate collection pockets for publication consent and private feedback. Participation should take under a minute away from the service queue.

This assumes some visitors value a concrete record of what changed. It may feel forced when nothing useful emerged, so “nothing clear yet” must remain an equally acceptable ending. The ritual celebrates careful inquiry without claiming every failure is beneficial.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate short handback periods offering either an ordinary repair summary or that summary plus the optional slip. In both periods, offer anonymous exit ticks: “I learned something useful: yes/unsure/no” and “The handback made me feel embarrassed or pressured: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes handback time and whether declined offers are accepted immediately, without recording identities. Inspect whether completed slips contain a specific observation rather than compulsory positivity. The idea is weakened if learning responses resemble the comparator while embarrassment, pressure, or delays increase. Low response numbers and self-selection limit conclusions; do not treat uptake as proof of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Open Questions Board
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Celebrate failed attempts by treating them as contributions to the café’s shared understanding of uncertainty. The mechanism is collective sense-making: an unresolved item can reveal a recurring question worth investigating, without putting its owner on display.

Before the event, volunteers turn permitted repair notes into three or four anonymous, non-procedural questions, such as “What information was missing before diagnosis?” or “When did we recognize that this repair exceeded our facilities?” Each card includes an honest statement of what remains unknown. Avoid item descriptions that could identify someone.

Visitors may silently read the board, place a pencil mark beside a question that helped them understand their own visit, or submit a new question on paper. Nothing requires describing their repair publicly. New submissions need a separate publication-consent tick and volunteer review. The closing ritual is a handwritten board footer: “These questions are worth carrying forward,” followed by one or two questions selected for relevance and safe scope, without vote totals or rankings. No promise of a future answer is made.

One volunteer prepares the initial cards, one checks proposed additions during quiet periods, and all four continue their ordinary repair roles. Reading and marking happen at the table edge after handback, outside the queue.

This assumes shared uncertainty can reduce isolation and support learning. It could instead resemble a catalogue of inadequacy or invite speculative technical advice. Keep all cards about observations, information needs, and service limits; omit repair instructions and unsupported explanations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Display the same permitted note summaries first as plain anonymous accounts and then as open questions, switching order midway through the event if practical. Offer separate optional paper responses: “What, if anything, did this help you understand?” and “Did this display make failed repairs feel more acceptable, unchanged, or more uncomfortable?” Observe congestion and whether visitors can bypass it easily. Compare the specificity of learning responses and reported discomfort between versions. The mechanism is doubtful if questions generate only vague approval, greater discomfort, or unsafe advice submissions. Different visitors and time periods make this a small design check, not causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Thank the Care, Leave the Outcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a private acknowledgment ritual to separate appreciation of a repair attempt from whether it succeeded. The mechanism is relational: a visitor can feel respected when someone recognizes a specific act of care, without having to reinterpret disappointment as success.

At handback, a volunteer may offer a folded paper card: “Would you like a short acknowledgment of the attempt? Passing is fine.” Inside, the volunteer writes one truthful, observable contribution, such as “You explained the fault clearly” or “We stopped when we reached the limits of our equipment.” Avoid praising persistence indiscriminately, assigning blame, or implying that stopping proves a repair was safe. The visitor can keep, decline, or discard it without explanation. There is no public reading.

A separate optional slip asks, “What care or effort would you like this café to recognize?” Visitors may acknowledge listening, patience, clear explanations, or respecting a decision to stop. With explicit permission, volunteers summarize these themes anonymously on the board under “Care we noticed today.” The board contains neither identifiable repair stories nor individual credits. This makes celebration visible while keeping personal acknowledgment private.

Four volunteers agree on a few factual wording examples before opening. Cards are completed only when handback allows; otherwise a visitor can take a blank reflection card to the table. One volunteer checks board contributions during a lull. Existing notes are unnecessary.

The approach assumes recognition feels supportive. It may seem patronizing, especially after a frustrating visit, and it does not itself establish technical learning. The offer must be brief, sincere, and easy to refuse.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare ordinary handbacks with handbacks offering the private acknowledgment during alternating short periods. Give both groups optional anonymous exit questions: “I felt respected,” “I can name something learned or a limit clarified,” and “I felt expected to be positive,” each with yes/unsure/no options. Observe added handback time, repeated offers after refusal, and any queue obstruction. A useful result would combine respect with identifiable learning or clearer limits, without increased pressure. Reject or revise the ritual if appreciation rises but pressure also rises, or if visitors describe it as patronizing. Sparse feedback leaves uncertainty; silence and acceptance are not evidence of comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Volunteers Go First
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make volunteers’ own unsuccessful attempts visible before inviting any visitor contribution. The mechanism is norm-setting through example: when the people treated as experts acknowledge uncertainty and disappointment without self-mockery, visitors may feel less personally judged by an unsuccessful repair.

Before opening, each willing volunteer writes a short anonymous account of an attempt they personally made: “We hoped… / What happened… / What changed in our understanding…” Use only truthful accounts they consent to share. Include unresolved disappointment where appropriate; do not manufacture a lesson. Exclude identifying item details, repair instructions, and claims that an item is safe. Two accounts are enough if others prefer to pass.

Display these under “Our attempts sometimes end here too.” At handback, a volunteer can briefly point out that the board is optional reading, without asking the visitor to contribute or respond. Beside it, provide folded paper headed “Something I wish repair volunteers understood about an unsuccessful visit.” Visitors can deposit an anonymous private note without speaking. These notes remain private and are not added to the display.

During a quiet moment near closing, the four volunteers read the notes and write one collective acknowledgment on the board, such as “A disappointing outcome can still deserve a clear explanation.” This closes the ritual without displaying visitors’ experiences or requiring positive feelings.

The table, paper, and board suffice; preparation takes a few minutes, and reading happens beyond the queue. The approach assumes volunteer examples feel credible and relatable. It could instead undermine confidence or make visitors feel responsible for comforting volunteers. Keep accounts brief, avoid excuses, and never seek reassurance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot during one event with alternating display periods: a neutral description of the café’s repair limits versus the volunteer accounts. Offer the same optional anonymous exit slip in both periods: “An unsuccessful repair would make me feel judged here: yes/unsure/no”; “Something this helped me understand: ___”; and “I felt asked to reassure volunteers: yes/unsure/no.” A volunteer observes queue obstruction and whether people can bypass the display and decline feedback without another invitation. Revise or stop if the accounts increase reported judgment, solicit comforting responses, or produce reassurance without identifiable learning. Different visitors, timing, and voluntary responses prevent a causal conclusion; uptake alone does not show comfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A Failed Attempt Changes Our Welcome
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Give unsuccessful attempts a concrete consequence in how the café operates. The mechanism is visible institutional responsiveness: an attempt becomes useful because the café changes a small practice in response, rather than asking its owner to find a positive meaning in the outcome.

Before the event, volunteers review existing repair notes that may be summarized anonymously. Choose one recurring, well-supported communication problem associated with unsuccessful visits—for example, visitors not knowing which equipment the café lacks. Do not infer a recurring problem from a single ambiguous note. Agree on one modest change achievable with paper, such as placing a plain-language facilities notice at the table.

Put a two-part card on the display board: “Earlier unsuccessful attempts showed us…” and “Today we changed…” Describe the communication gap and actual change without identifying visitors, blaming anyone, or giving technical repair advice. Label it “An attempt that changed the café.” This is the celebratory act: publicly crediting unsuccessful work with improving the service, without naming its participants or suggesting their disappointment was necessary.

After handback, anyone may silently leave a private slip completing “One thing that would have made today clearer…” Submission is optional and separate from service. A publication-consent box permits an anonymous summary, but private feedback remains useful without that permission. During a lull, volunteers may implement one feasible clarification and update the board only after doing so. If nothing suitable emerges, leave the original change visible rather than inventing progress.

All four volunteers retain their repair roles; one checks slips during quiet periods. This requires authority to make small communication changes and enough permitted notes to identify a genuine issue. It cannot compensate for a poor repair explanation, and the board could feel promotional unless it states the change modestly and honestly.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For a small prototype, alternate between displaying the new facilities notice alone and displaying it with the anonymous account of why it changed. Keep the actual service improvement available throughout. Offer optional exit ticks: “I understand this café’s limits”; “Unsuccessful attempts seem useful to improving this café”; and “This framing made my disappointment feel dismissed,” each with yes/unsure/no, plus space for an example of something learned. Observe congestion, unobstructed opt-out, and whether volunteers pursue declined feedback. The proposed mechanism is weakened if the origin story adds no understanding or usefulness, or increases dismissal. Inspect whether the promised change actually happened. One event provides a practical design check, with substantial uncertainty from small numbers and self-selection.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Hindsight Fold
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Turn a permitted account of an unsuccessful repair into a silent, folded-paper exercise that lets visitors experience how uncertainty changes with information. The mechanism is perspective-taking: an outcome can look obvious afterward, while an honest reconstruction shows why the attempt was informative.

Before the event, two volunteers select one existing repair note with permission for anonymous summarization. It must document both an initial uncertainty and something the attempt actually established. If no note supports that sequence, do not manufacture one. Remove identifying details and all procedural repair advice.

The outside of a folded sheet gives the initial situation in broad terms and asks: “Could you tell whether a repair would be possible from this information?” Readers can privately consider “yes,” “no,” or “unsure,” without submitting an answer. Inside, reveal the documented outcome and the specific information gained. Include “The item remained unrepaired” plainly. The final line reads: “This attempt gave us a case worth learning from. Disappointment can remain.” There is no correct-answer score, public response, or invitation to diagnose the item.

Place a few copies at the table edge, clear of the queue. The board holds the same folded case under “An unsuccessful attempt, a useful lesson.” Opening the fold is the optional ritual; visitors need neither speak nor contribute their own experience. Two volunteers prepare and check the wording before opening; all four retain their ordinary roles during service.

This assumes the notes preserve enough information to reconstruct uncertainty faithfully. A selective account could excuse poor work or exaggerate learning. Use modest claims and omit cases whose educational value depends on technical instructions.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one event, alternate the folded version with an unfolded version containing exactly the same account. Offer optional anonymous slips asking: “What did this attempt establish?”, “Did this make unsuccessful repairs feel less shameful, unchanged, or more shameful?”, and “Did you feel tested or pressured?” Observe obstruction and whether visitors can ignore the display without prompting. Stop or revise if the fold attracts guessing but yields no clearer learning, increases embarrassment, or delays service. Sparse, self-selected feedback cannot establish effectiveness; inspect unanswered and critical responses alongside favorable ones.

EXPAND.title: One Attempt Changes the Café
EXPAND.proposal:
Make a failed attempt valuable by using it to change one café practice. The mechanism is visible institutional learning: visitors see that an unresolved repair can improve the service, without having to describe their own experience as positive.

Before opening, the four volunteers use permitted anonymous notes to identify one recurring, nontechnical problem they can address immediately—for example, visitors discovering the café’s equipment limits only at handback. Put a folded sheet on the table: “An unsuccessful attempt showed us…” inside, followed by “Today we changed…” A suitable change might be explaining those limits at arrival. The small board displays the same pair and the invitation: “Thank you for helping us improve, including when repairs remain unfinished.” Include no identifying details or repair instructions.

After handback, visitors can optionally submit a paper suggestion: “Something the café could explain or organize differently.” No speaking is required. Suggestions remain private unless a separate box explicitly permits anonymous display. During a quiet moment, the designated review volunteer checks suggestions with a second volunteer. They may enact only changes within existing resources and agreed service procedures; safety procedures and technical repair decisions are outside this ritual. Unworkable suggestions receive no public promise. At closing, record one enacted change, or honestly state that none was identified.

This needs paper, the board, and a short opening agreement. It assumes at least one useful service change is available. It can otherwise become empty symbolism or make visitors feel responsible for improving the café. Keep the invitation away from the queue and remove any contribution on request.
EXPAND.experiment: The review volunteer owns a one-event pilot. Compare short periods using the prior “Still broken; now we know…” slip with periods showing an actual café change; alternate their order. Offer both groups anonymous exit ticks for useful learning, embarrassment or pressure, and an optional example of what they learned. Observe queue obstruction and whether refusals end the invitation immediately. Check that the advertised change actually happened. This challenger shows no improvement if learning is no clearer than with the slip, or if service feedback creates more pressure. Stop invitations if they delay handback or visitors report feeling obliged to contribute; withdraw any unsupported change claim immediately. Small, self-selected responses cannot establish superiority.

EXPAND.title: Guess, Unfold, Learn
EXPAND.proposal:
Turn an anonymous failed attempt into a tiny prediction puzzle. The mechanism is surprise followed by correction: discovering that a plausible expectation was wrong can make uncertainty memorable without exposing the current visitor’s repair.

Before the event, two volunteers select two permitted repair notes that clearly document an initial uncertainty and what the attempt actually established. Do not invent a cause, a test result, or a successful ending. Make folded paper cards with an initial situation and two plausible predictions outside, then the recorded observation inside. Use nontechnical distinctions such as “Did having a clear symptom description settle what was wrong, or did uncertainty remain?” If the notes do not support a fair question and answer, do not use that example.

Place the cards at the table edge after the service queue. A sign says: “An unfinished repair taught us this. Guess silently, then unfold. Passing is welcome.” Visitors make their prediction mentally; nobody records scores. Inside each card, show the observation, the remaining uncertainty, and “Thanks to the attempt that made this clearer.” The board holds one large example. No prizes, rankings, names, photographs, or repair steps appear.

One volunteer checks cards during ordinary quiet moments; all four retain their repair duties. Visitors leave cards on the table and may leave immediately. Retire confusing examples instead of improvising explanations in a crowded queue.

The route assumes the notes contain an understandable discrepancy between expectation and observation. It teaches through another case, so transfer to the visitor’s own disappointment is uncertain. Avoid trick questions, which could recreate shame around being wrong.
EXPAND.experiment: A designated card volunteer owns a one-event comparison between folded prediction cards and the same cases presented as straightforward summaries. Switch formats halfway through, acknowledging that visitor groups differ. Optional anonymous slips ask what the case clarified, whether unfinished repairs now feel more acceptable, and whether the activity felt like being tested. Observe bypass access and congestion. The mechanism is weakened if prediction cards yield no more specific understanding than summaries, or increase embarrassment. Remove a card immediately if its answer is disputed or unsupported; stop the activity if it obstructs the queue or repeatedly feels evaluative. Do not interpret card handling or correct guesses as evidence of learning.

EXPAND.title: The Volunteers Go First
EXPAND.proposal:
Have the café’s volunteers model acknowledging their own unsuccessful work. The mechanism is a change in the perceived social norm: people with repair expertise visibly treat a reasonable but unsuccessful attempt as discussable, reducing the sense that visitors alone must explain failure.

Before opening, volunteers may privately contribute one short, truthful account of their own repair work: “We expected… What happened was… What we would explain differently now…” Participation by volunteers is optional too. Use a collective account only with explicit permission from everyone whose experience it represents. Remove names, distinctive item details, blame, and procedural advice. Existing notes may support factual checking where their permitted use covers this purpose; do not attribute somebody else’s story to the volunteers.

Put one account on the board under “Our unfinished work belongs here too.” The ritual is simply turning over a folded paper panel at the start of the event to reveal the account. It needs no audience or speech. Visitors can read it after handback, pass it, or privately tick “I would welcome more accounts like this.” They are never invited to match the disclosure with their own story.

A designated volunteer checks wording before display and removes it if consent changes. Another checks that the account does not suggest the café ignores safety or treats avoidable errors casually. If nobody wishes to contribute, omit the ritual; do not pressure staff into vulnerability.

This requires only the board and paper. Its key assumption is that volunteers’ example carries social credibility. It may instead lower confidence in the service, and an admission alone does not guarantee useful learning. Include a concrete, supported lesson about uncertainty or communication.
EXPAND.experiment: The display volunteer owns a one-event pilot. Compare periods showing the volunteer account with periods showing an equally brief anonymous case and the same lesson. Use optional paper responses about useful understanding, comfort with an unfinished repair, and confidence in the café. Observe whether visitors bypass the display freely and whether reading creates congestion. This route fails its practical test if comfort does not improve, learning stays vague, or confidence falls without a corresponding benefit. Remove the account immediately after a consent withdrawal or credible identification concern; stop the display if it prompts distress or disrupts service. A handful of favorable comments supports revision, not a claim that shame has been reduced.

EXPAND.title: Let the Owner Teach One Thing
EXPAND.proposal:
Offer a visitor whose repair remains unfinished a brief chance to teach the café something about living with the item. The mechanism is role reversal: the owner becomes a source of useful knowledge instead of remaining only the recipient of an unsuccessful service.

Before opening, volunteers agree on a single optional prompt: “You know this item in everyday use. Is there one thing you wish repair volunteers understood about that experience?” Put it on paper at the table edge, away from handback. Examples concern use and priorities—such as why an intermittent problem is difficult to describe—not instructions for repairing or operating a potentially unsafe item.

At handback, a volunteer can point once to the prompt. The visitor may write, say nothing, or leave. The form has separate choices: “For volunteers only” and “You may display an anonymous summary.” Neither is preselected. A volunteer reads submissions during a lull and writes a short response on the same sheet: “This helps us understand…” only when they can state a genuine implication. The visitor may collect it before leaving but need not wait. With explicit permission, one reviewed contribution goes on the board under “What owners taught us today.” No identities, photos, procedural advice, or comparative praise appear.

One volunteer owns the paper review while the other three maintain normal roles; review pauses whenever repair work requires all four. Private sheets are not displayed and are discarded after the event. Remove a displayed contribution on request.

This assumes some owners want to contribute experiential knowledge. Others may feel asked to perform unpaid emotional work after disappointment. The invitation must not imply that receiving respectful service depends on teaching, and an unreviewed contribution must not be presented as learning already achieved.
EXPAND.experiment: The review volunteer owns a one-event comparison with a simple optional “Tell us about your visit” sheet. Alternate the two prompts across short periods. Offer a separate anonymous check: “Did you feel knowledgeable and respected?”, “Did you learn anything useful?”, and “Did this feel like extra work or pressure?” Inspect whether volunteers can accurately state a new understanding from the teaching submissions. The route is weakened if contributions yield no clearer learning than general feedback, or increase burden and embarrassment. Stop offers when review creates a backlog, handback slows, or a visitor feels obliged to help. Check that declines receive no second invitation. Self-selection and sparse responses leave the effect uncertain.

EXPAND.title: A Useful Ending — improved learning-record mechanism (source: prior candidate 0)
EXPAND.proposal:
An unfinished repair can leave behind a truthful, useful record. Preserve the source mechanism, but have the volunteer supply the factual observation before inviting reflection, and make acknowledgment optional. This removes the requirement that a disappointed owner invent a lesson.

Before opening, the four volunteers agree on permissible statements: documented observations, unresolved questions, and limits of the café’s facilities. One volunteer owns the pilot and reviews shared material during quiet periods; everyone retains normal repair duties.

At handback, offer once: “Would you like a note of what this attempt established? Passing is fine.” If accepted, write one supported observation and what remains unknown. The owner may silently mark “useful,” “unclear,” or leave it blank and keep it. If nothing was established, write “Unresolved today”; offer ordinary handback without a learning card as an equally valid ending. Never imply that stopping establishes an item’s safety.

A separate, unselected consent box permits an anonymous board summary. Review every summary for identifying details and unsafe advice. The board says “Thank you for helping us find out,” without counts or individual credit. Permitted existing notes may supply initial examples, clearly identified as earlier records. No names or photos are collected.

This requires paper, the board, and brief preparation. Its assumption is that a factual record can validate an attempt without demanding optimism. If volunteers cannot establish a supported observation, skip the learning claim. If review capacity disappears, keep cards private and pause board additions.
EXPAND.experiment: For one event, the pilot owner alternates short blocks using the source’s owner-completed prompt and the revised volunteer-completed offer. Both remain optional. After handback, offer a separate anonymous slip: “Something became clearer,” “I felt pressure to make this positive,” and “I preferred to pass.” Record offers, refusals, approximate handback delay, and queue interruptions without identities. Check that declining ends the invitation immediately. Stop the pilot for an ignored refusal, unsafe wording, or repeated queue interruption. The revision shows no gain if clarity does not improve, or pressure or delay increases; small, self-selected responses cannot establish superiority.

EXPAND.title: Choose the Question Before the Outcome
EXPAND.proposal:
Move the learning criterion before the repair attempt. The mechanism is prospective expectation setting: an unsuccessful repair may answer a question the owner already cared about, reducing pressure to invent value afterward.

Before opening, prepare folded paper with two private prompts: “Besides getting it working, something I would like to understand is…” and “After the attempt: answered / partly answered / still open.” Display a sample blank on the small board with “An unanswered question is welcome too.” Do not prescribe technical questions or promise answers.

While waiting, visitors may take a sheet, write a question, and keep it folded. Participation requires no speaking, and volunteers do not add a mandatory intake step. A visitor may show the question during the ordinary repair conversation; otherwise it stays private. Volunteers address it only within normal service time and their competence. Questions requiring unsafe investigation or unavailable expertise remain open and receive the café’s ordinary handoff explanation.

After handback, the owner can silently revisit the question at the table. The closing ritual is folding the sheet shut under the printed sentence, “Thank you for letting an attempt help us learn.” Keeping, discarding, or ignoring it are equally acceptable. No personal material is displayed or collected; the board celebrates the practice itself.

One volunteer owns supplies and observes use during lulls; the other three maintain ordinary duties, with all four available for repairs. If visitors arrive without waiting time, offer ordinary handback rather than reconstructing a supposedly prior question. This needs only paper and the board. It assumes some owners have a meaningful secondary question. It may instead burden them or feel like lowering expectations; success at repair remains the service goal.
EXPAND.experiment: At one monthly event, alternate brief periods with the prospective sheet available and periods with ordinary service and the same generic thank-you board. Offer both groups an optional anonymous exit slip asking whether an unfinished attempt clarified anything and whether they felt pressured to accept disappointment. The pilot owner records availability periods, uptake, refusals, and interruptions; check that passing triggers no follow-up. Stop for repeated intake delay, ignored opt-outs, or complaints that questions displaced repair attention. No increase in reported clarity, or increased pressure or service interruption, would count against this route. Treat results as a small feasibility check, especially if few repairs remain unfinished.
